authors.name: Rowan Vale
authors.bio: The man behind The Pecking Order. Rowan trades in sharp verdicts, spectacular reversals and an unwavering belief that this week finally explained everything. His inbox rarely agrees.

authors.name: Mara Voss
authors.bio: Mara follows the details that outlast the scoreboard: protection, personnel, responsibility and the choices that turn a talented roster into a contender.

authors.name: Ellis Quill
authors.bio: Ellis writes The Long Season, a column about the people and expectations beneath the standings. A bad afternoon is evidence, not a complete biography.

authors.name: Dorian Pike
authors.bio: Dorian asks the awkward question, counts the points and keeps asking. The Uncomfortable Truth takes the league’s overlooked clubs seriously.

authors.name: Tessa Wren
authors.bio: Tessa studies the matchups, names the pressure points and puts a score beside every pick. She covers the entire weekly slate for The Week Ahead.

authors.name: Calvin Rook
authors.bio: Calvin covers the college game and the next IFL class. The Rook Board is built around projection, athletic traits and the occasional prospect he refuses to stop believing in.

articles.title: Poury supplies the points; Mossdeep secures the bye
articles.dek: Holt scored through the air and on the ground in a 27–3 win over Sunyshore. The Eclipse are 15–0, with the conference’s first seed secured and a second-quarter review waiting.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Poury Holt caught a twelve-yard touchdown pass on Mossdeep’s first possession and ran seven yards for another score late in the third quarter. Between those plays, the Eclipse gave Sunyshore very little room to build an answer. Mossdeep won 27–3, improved to 15–0 and secured the Hoenn–Sinnoh conference’s first seed and postseason bye. The Starseekers left with 170 total yards, one field goal and a much clearer account of the work a return visit would require.

Holt finished with 121 yards on eighteen carries and caught all three of his targets for forty-seven more. Dram Marino completed twenty-one of twenty-six passes for 316 yards and two touchdowns, adding a one-yard rushing score. Ninjulio Jones caught six passes for 126 yards. Mossdeep converted five of seven third downs, produced twenty-two first downs and held the ball for the final 4:54 without allowing another Sunyshore possession.

Michael Dorrill had plenty to recognize. He also had two punts, an interception and a missed extra point to discuss. A scoreless second quarter had interrupted a thirteen-point opening period, leaving the visitors within ten at halftime. The Eclipse’s defense kept that interruption from becoming a serious threat, but Dorrill’s standards do not depend on the other team making him pay immediately.

“We earned the bye. Good. Now pull up the second quarter,” Dorrill said. “Two punts and a ball thrown to the other team. Everybody can enjoy the standings after they explain those possessions. We have two more games before the playoffs, and neither opponent is responsible for improving our execution.”
Holt made the early opportunities count

Mossdeep’s first offensive snap produced a forty-two-yard completion deep right from Marino to Accel BeckhmJr. Holt followed with two three-yard runs left, then caught the short-right throw on third-and-four for the opening touchdown at 4:07. A missed extra point kept the score at 6–0. The drive covered sixty yards in four plays and gave Sunyshore an immediate example of the problem: protecting against the deep receiver still left a useful back available underneath.

The next Eclipse possession traveled eighty-four yards in eight plays. Marino finished it himself, running up the middle from one yard with a minute left in the first quarter. Adam Vinathorn made the extra point for a 13–0 lead. Sunyshore had punted on its first two possessions and would punt again before the quarter ended. The Starseekers were already having to win several consecutive exchanges merely to get back into a competitive position.

Holt’s contribution deserves attention beyond the two scoring entries. His receiving gains came on three targets, so Mossdeep obtained forty-seven yards without an incompletion on those throws. His rushing work averaged 6.7 yards per carry. Those are distinct jobs, and he completed both against an opponent that entered the afternoon with eleven wins. Holt’s combination of rushing and receiving production helped Mossdeep sustain drives against one of the conference’s strongest opponents.

“If I’m carrying it, I expect to move us,” Holt said. “If the throw comes my way, I expect to finish the catch. Being useful in one part of the offense doesn’t excuse missing the other part.” It was a direct answer from a player whose afternoon made the claim easy to check.

body.text: Sunyshore earned its second-quarter stops

Don Philliams brought Marino down for a five-yard loss on second-and-one at the start of the second quarter. Scol Alexander broke up the following deep-right throw to BeckhmJr, forcing Mossdeep’s first punt. The Starseekers had turned an apparently favorable down for the offense into a defensive stop. That is a sequence Karson Jones can use in preparation without pretending the complete performance met the same standard.

The next Mossdeep possession included a twenty-one-yard completion to BeckhmJr on third-and-nine. It also included a Shawn Mareman fumble recovered by teammate Gronkaludon, another Alexander breakup and a Mareman run stopped for a loss. Vinathorn punted again. Mossdeep retained the fumble, so the turnover ledger correctly shows no lost fumbles for either club; the possession still contained mistakes Dorrill has reason to revisit.

Marino then moved the Eclipse forty-four yards before a deep-right pass was intercepted by Castform with fifty-nine seconds remaining in the half. Sunyshore advanced thirty-three yards on the ensuing possession, and Ampharos made a sixty-yard field goal with eleven seconds left. That kick supplied all three Starseekers points. Their defense had created an opening, and Ampharos finished the possession with a sixty-yard kick.

“You can see the standard in those stops,” Jones said. “Now you have to carry it into the next series, and the offense has to make something of it. I’m not sending those guys home thinking three points is who we are. I’m sending them home knowing what three points makes us fix.” Sunyshore’s five first-half punts help explain why the defensive work could only narrow the deficit.
Two third-quarter possessions settled the result

Mossdeep opened the second half with ten plays and eighty-one yards. Holt converted third-and-one with a ten-yard run up the middle during the possession. Marino found George Kipple short right for four yards on another snap, while Gronkaludon caught short-right throws for thirteen and nine. BeckhmJr finished the drive with a four-yard touchdown catch short left at 3:00, and Vinathorn’s kick made it 20–3.

Electric Berry intercepted DeZhaun Watzon’s deep-left pass on Sunyshore’s next possession and returned it eleven yards. The Eclipse needed six plays to cover the remaining fifty-two yards. Marino converted third-and-one with a two-yard run, then found Jones deep middle for thirty-two. Holt eventually scored up the middle from seven yards with thirteen seconds left in the quarter. Mossdeep had added fourteen points while the visitors remained on three.

Jones caught every pass directed his way. His thirty-two-yard reception on that scoring possession was the largest of his six catches, but his later twenty-seven-yarder would solve another difficult down. BeckhmJr finished with four catches for seventy-eight yards and a score; Gronkaludon caught six for fifty-six. The distribution matters because Sunyshore did produce three pass breakups from Alexander and two sacks from Philliams. A few successful individual matchups did not close the other available routes.

“The next throw matters more than explaining the last one,” Marino said. “We had a bad finish to the first half. The answer was to complete the next possession properly.” His twenty-one completions and one interception support a good overall passing afternoon, while leaving room for the specific correction the coach will demand.
The defense and the final 4:54

Joey Sporeter recorded two sacks and seven pressures. Will Shells supplied the third sack, and Watzon finished thirteen of twenty-six for 122 yards with one interception. Myles Gabite ran twelve times for forty-eight yards; the Starseekers’ entire rushing total was also forty-eight. Sunyshore converted three of ten third downs and finished with nine first downs. Fera LaGatr’s five catches for fifty-six yards led the receiving group.

The visitors’ final possession traveled sixty-one yards in ten plays but ended on downs. Mossdeep took over with 4:54 left and never returned the ball. Holt opened with runs of thirteen and fifteen yards. Philliams later sacked Marino for six, creating third-and-sixteen; Marino answered with the twenty-seven-yard deep-right completion to Jones. A later fourteen-yard Holt run renewed the downs again, and the last recorded carry left the Eclipse close to the goal line as time expired.

body.alt: Ninjask #46, Serperior #39. Ninjulio Jones gained twenty-seven yards on third-and-sixteen during Mossdeep’s final possession.
body.caption: Ninjulio Jones gained twenty-seven yards on third-and-sixteen during Mossdeep’s final possession.

body.text: That final drive covered eighty yards without adding points. It was valuable because Sunyshore had no further opportunity to reduce the margin. Mossdeep did not have to ask its defense for another stop or expose the result to a sequence of quick possessions. Jones’ third-down catch was especially useful: it preserved the drive after one of the visitors’ best defensive plays.

Sunyshore is now 11–4 and heads to Pastoria with its division title already secured. Mossdeep hosts Sootopolis before closing at Lavaridge. The bye allows the Eclipse to know where their postseason begins, but it does not settle who they will face or how cleanly they will play. Holt’s two scores, Jones’ perfect six-target afternoon and a defense that conceded no touchdowns supplied the victory. The two punts and the intercepted pass remain available for Dorrill’s next meeting.

articles.title: Lamb goes for 350 as Saffron overwhelms Blackthorn, 70–0
articles.dek: Archam Manning threw seven touchdown passes, HeeDee Lamb caught five of them, and NeMarcus Tare recorded seven sacks. A stunned division leader now has to recover before Mahogany.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: HeeDee Lamb caught thirteen passes for 350 yards and five touchdowns. Archam Manning threw for 528 yards and seven scores. NeMarcus Tare recorded seven sacks. Saffron beat Blackthorn 70–0, and every attempt to summarize the afternoon seems to omit another number that would ordinarily lead a game report. The Dragons arrived as an eleven-win club. They left without a point and with ten sacks charged to their quarterback.

Saffron improved to 12–3, while Blackthorn fell to 11–4. The Psi Corps scored twenty-eight points in the second quarter and another twenty-eight in the fourth. Their 648 total yards exceeded the Dragons’ 179 by 469. They made twenty first downs to Blackthorn’s six, converted six of ten third downs and punted once. Octillery made all ten extra points, providing the afternoon’s most repetitive job description.

The timing made the result especially striking. Saffron had lost 36–33 at Mt. Silver the previous week after an enormous comeback ended with a late field goal. Tare recorded seven sacks in that game too. This time the pressure came with an offense that repeatedly finished possessions and a defense that never surrendered a scoring answer. The same pass rusher had a much more comfortable scoreboard to consult.

“I wanted them to bring the effort back and clean up what hurt us,” Trent Scarboro said. “That’s what I’m proud of. The receiver finishing, the quarterback putting it there, the guys getting home, everybody helping the next guy do his job. You don’t get a day like this from one player, even when one player’s line looks like that.”
The first quarter gave little warning of seventy

Saffron led only 7–0 after the opening period. Gengar Pickens scored on a four-yard run right to complete an eight-play, sixty-nine-yard drive. Blackthorn had punted on its first two possessions, with Pawmo and Tare each recording a third-down sack. The Psi Corps then punted themselves after a drive gained no yards. There was still a recognizable game, with the visitors one successful possession away from changing its direction.

Blackthorn’s next series traveled twenty-eight yards and ended with a missed field goal early in the second quarter. That would be its only field-goal attempt. Saffron responded with a six-play, fifty-two-yard drive, finished by Dam Skattebo’s eight-yard run left at 3:55. The score became 14–0. The Dragons still had time to recover, but their next possessions put them back in precisely the situations Tare was already exploiting.

The shutout therefore did not require Saffron to score on every opportunity. Its lone punt came while the game was still close, and Blackthorn had a kick to put points on the board. The difference grew when Saffron turned successive stops into touchdowns while the visitors continued surrendering possessions. A scoreboard this large can obscure the period when the next stop or completion would still have mattered considerably.
Three Lamb touchdowns before the break

Manning was sacked for five yards at the start of Saffron’s next scoring possession. On second-and-fifteen, he threw deep left to Lamb for an eighty-five-yard touchdown. The drive lasted two plays. Blackthorn had created the long-yardage down and then surrendered the longest reception of Lamb’s afternoon. It was an immediate, costly failure to convert a defensive success into a completed stop.

body.alt: Alakazam #6, Heliolisk #11. Archam Manning and HeeDee Lamb connected on an eighty-five-yard touchdown pass.
body.caption: Archam Manning and HeeDee Lamb connected on an eighty-five-yard touchdown pass.

body.text: The Dragons went backward on their next possession and punted. Manning threw incomplete on the first play of Saffron’s answer, then found Lamb deep right for a forty-eight-yard touchdown at 1:42. Another Blackthorn series began with a seven-yard Tare sack and ended with a punt. Saffron now had the ball with 1:16 left and enough time to add another touchdown before halftime.

That third scoring drive was longer: seven plays and sixty-two yards. On fourth-and-three, with nine seconds remaining, Manning found Lamb deep right for twenty-four yards and another score. The extra point made it 35–0. In less than two and a half minutes of game clock, Lamb had scored from eighty-five, forty-eight and twenty-four yards. Two of those receptions came on the right; the first had gone left. Blackthorn was losing the matchup across the field.

“The distances change. The catch still has to be finished,” Lamb said. “Archam put the ball where I could work. I tried to keep the next route as clean as the last one.” His calm explanation was considerably shorter than the list of touchdowns. The thirteen catches came on seventeen targets, leaving him room to discuss four unsuccessful throws if Scarboro needed another meeting topic.
Tare kept removing the next possession

Tare’s seven sacks came with thirteen pressures. Chen Norton Jr added two sacks and four pressures, while Pawmo contributed a sack of his own. Hatterene finished fifteen of twenty-eight for 154 yards, threw two interceptions and took all ten sacks. The passing-yard total and sack losses are separate recorded figures; the Dragons’ offense was being pushed backward in addition to struggling to complete its throws.

The fourth-quarter sequences were particularly punishing. Tare sacked Hatterene on first-and-ten and then again on fourth-and-one during a possession that ended on downs. Norton recorded sacks on consecutive snaps of the following Blackthorn series. After Saffron lost a Skattebo fumble, Tare answered with sacks on first-and-ten and second-and-seventeen. The Dragons could force a turnover and still find themselves punting within a few plays.

body.alt: Ninetales #42, Hatterene #12. NeMarcus Tare recorded seven sacks against Blackthorn.
body.caption: NeMarcus Tare recorded seven sacks against Blackthorn.

body.text: Blackthorn converted only two of twelve third downs. Its nine rushing attempts produced twenty-five yards, with Sawsbuck gaining fourteen on three carries before appearing on the injury report. Tinkaton supplied six catches for seventy-four yards, the clearest productive receiving line on an otherwise grim offensive sheet. Those completions never became a touchdown drive, and the defense was repeatedly returned to the field against Manning and Lamb.

“Our protection has to give the offense a chance to finish a series,” Clair said. “The score is there for everybody to read. We need to be exact about what happened before each possession ended.” There is plenty to examine without pretending every sack had the same cause or assigning a missed responsibility the record does not identify.
Saffron continued finding different finishers

Pawmo caught a sixteen-yard touchdown pass short left on Saffron’s opening drive of the third quarter. Jolt Train Ln then intercepted Hatterene and returned the ball thirty-one yards. The Psi Corps used twelve plays to cover forty yards on the ensuing possession, with Skattebo scoring from two yards on the first snap of the fourth quarter. The pace varied; the scoring outcome did not.

Manning’s other sack also preceded an immediate touchdown answer. Whiscash brought him down for eight yards, making it second-and-eighteen. Manning found Mothel Irving deep left for forty-six yards and a score on the next snap. Irving caught all five of his targets for 114 yards. With Lamb commanding the largest share of attention, Saffron still obtained another hundred-yard receiving performance and a touchdown from a different player.

Lamb added touchdown catches of twenty-six and twenty-four yards in the final sixty-one seconds. Between them, Seadra fumbled after a short completion and Kecleon recovered for Saffron. Jolt Train Ln intercepted Blackthorn’s final pass as well. Manning finished twenty-five of thirty-three without an interception. Skattebo ran for eighty-two yards and two scores; Pickens’ opening rushing touchdown completed the three ground scores alongside seven through the air.

The final report lists Sawsbuck with six weeks of injury recovery remaining. Saffron’s Skattebo and Tare appear with minor entries in the game record, which should not be inflated into a longer absence or a diagnosis. Blackthorn’s immediate concern is the trip to Mahogany and a division race that remains open. Saffron goes to Cerulean, still pursuing the conference’s top seed while Mt. Silver retains control of its own route to the bye.

Seventy points will move opinions, including mine. It should also leave the specific evidence visible: explosive throws after sacks, seven passing touchdowns, relentless pressure and no Blackthorn touchdown to interrupt the sequence. Saffron has supplied an emphatic response to last week’s defeat. Blackthorn now has two regular-season games to supply one of its own.

art.alt: Heliolisk #11. HeeDee Lamb caught five touchdown passes in Saffron’s 70–0 victory.

articles.title: Lavender scores twenty-two in the fourth and leaves Cerulean with its tenth win
articles.dek: Machoke finishes two long drives, Blathers supplies the late interception, and Hobbes runs for 122 yards in a 32–21 comeback.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Lavender began the fourth quarter eleven points behind, having punted on all three of its third-quarter possessions. Cerulean had the larger passing plays, the lead and a road opponent whose available offense was still learning how much work it could share. The Wails then scored twenty-two unanswered points, won 32–21 and left with their tenth victory. It was a convincing final quarter after a long stretch that had offered very little comfort.

Machoke caught the touchdown that began the recovery and ran for the one that put Lavender ahead. Blathers intercepted Farigiraf on the next Cerulean possession and returned it thirty-nine yards. Hobbes finished the resulting short field with his second rushing touchdown. Those three scoring drives arrived within the same quarter, but they did different jobs: first restore a competitive game, then take the lead, then make Cerulean chase two scores.

“We finished some drives,” Travis Scarboro said. Asked what changed after the third-quarter punts, he added, “Completions. Blocks. Converted the try. Got the ball back.” The answer was characteristically economical, and the recorded sequence supported every item. Lavender scored touchdowns on drives of seventy-seven and eighty-one yards before the interception gave it the final six-yard assignment.
Hobbes gave Lavender an early foundation

The Wails opened with an eighty-one-yard touchdown drive that consumed fourteen recorded plays and a little more than four minutes. Frosmoth found Luvdisc for seventeen yards on third-and-five, Samurott for thirteen after an incompletion, and several shorter completions that helped the runners keep working. Hobbes finished with a five-yard run left at 1:59 of the first quarter. Lavender had made a patient start without asking its passing game to produce one enormous play.

body.alt: Arcanine #58. Hobbes carried twenty times for 122 yards in Lavender’s comeback.
body.caption: Hobbes carried twenty times for 122 yards in Lavender’s comeback.

body.text: Cerulean answered immediately enough to keep the opening possession from defining the half. Farigiraf connected with Zebstrika for thirty-two yards, found Raticate for nineteen on third-and-five and moved the ball to Bibarel for a six-yard touchdown with five seconds left in the quarter. The Tide had covered seventy-seven yards on their own scoring drive. Both teams had demonstrated a route to the end zone, and neither could count on having the more comfortable afternoon.

Just a cactus gave Lavender a 10–7 lead with a fifty-one-yard field goal in the second quarter. Picasso then intercepted Farigiraf’s deep-right attempt and returned it twelve yards. Lavender could not turn that chance into more points: Wugtrio intercepted Frosmoth’s deep-right throw on third-and-eleven, returning it twelve yards as well. The two interceptions came a minute apart on the game clock and left neither offense entitled to a lecture about the other’s caution.

Cerulean used its next possession much more profitably. Arctozolt gained thirty-seven yards on a short-middle completion, and Farigiraf later found Delcatty for seventeen on third-and-seven. A three-yard touchdown pass to Wiglett put the Tide ahead 14–10 just before halftime. That drive traveled ninety-six yards. Cerulean had built its lead through substantial offensive work, which made Lavender’s eventual recovery more impressive than a summary of the final score alone would suggest.
Zebstrika opened an eleven-point lead

The third quarter offered Lavender several defensive successes and almost no offensive reward. Mauler Twin sacked Farigiraf for an eight-yard loss on Cerulean’s opening possession of the half. Later, Muk stopped Glalie for no gain on third-and-one, and Throh broke up the fourth-down pass intended for Marowak. The Wails had supplied opportunities for their offense to change the game, but the next Lavender possession also ended in a punt.

At 1:44, Farigiraf threw deep over the middle to Zebstrika for an eighty-yard touchdown. Torterra’s extra point made it 21–10. Zebstrika finished with five catches for 134 yards, so the long score accounted for much of a dangerous receiving afternoon without being his only contribution. Farigiraf would finish with 302 yards and three touchdown passes. Lavender had to contend with actual explosive production, not merely survive an opponent waiting to make a mistake.

body.alt: Zebstrika #24. Zebstrika scored on an eighty-yard reception before Lavender’s fourth-quarter rally.
body.caption: Zebstrika scored on an eighty-yard reception before Lavender’s fourth-quarter rally.

body.text: The Wails punted again after the touchdown. Machoke gained four yards on first down, Unfezant caught a three-yard pass, and a third-and-three run went nowhere. At that point I would have understood any Lavender supporter who preferred to study the next opponent’s schedule. The team had ten points, three consecutive punts and a deficit that required more than one successful possession. Its subsequent response deserves to be measured against that position.
Might Guy and Hobbes restart the offense

Frosmoth opened the fourth-quarter recovery with a deep-right completion to Might Guy for thirty-two yards. Hobbes followed with runs of ten, nine and nine yards, moving the drive forward without a third-down interruption. Wailord added a fourteen-yard catch, and the Wails eventually reached third-and-two. Frosmoth threw short right to Machoke for the touchdown at 4:16.

The two-point attempt was important enough to keep separate from the touchdown in the account. Frosmoth again threw short right, this time to Beedrill, and the try succeeded. Lavender trailed 21–18. A field goal could now tie the game, though the Wails would not need to settle for one. The drive had combined a large opening completion, several useful runs and a short finishing throw; it was the most complete evidence yet that the available offense could function together.

“I wanted the next call before anybody finished celebrating,” Frosmoth said. “We had more work. The first completion helped, and then Hobbes kept giving us the next down.” The quick, impatient answer suited a passer whose fourth quarter improved the meaning of his full line. He finished nineteen of thirty-one for 201 yards, one touchdown and one interception. The total is modest beside Farigiraf’s, but the timing of Lavender’s completions became decisive.

Cerulean gained nineteen yards through Delcatty on the next possession, then threw three consecutive incompletions and punted. Lavender took over with 3:34 remaining. Might Guy again opened the drive with a substantial catch, this one twenty-seven yards deep left. Wailord and Luvdisc supplied the next completions, Hobbes ran for eight and twelve, and the Wails reached another short-yardage finishing opportunity.

Machoke scored on a five-yard run left on third-and-one at 2:02. Just a cactus made the extra point, and Lavender led 25–21. Machoke’s full rushing total was eighteen yards on six carries, but his receiving touchdown and go-ahead run made his contribution larger than that total appears in isolation. “They let me do the last bit twice,” he said. “I thought that was very considerate.” The pleasure in the joke was easier to understand than any attempt at modesty would have been.
Blathers gives the finish a shorter field

Cerulean still had time for a winning touchdown drive. Farigiraf completed a short pass to Zebstrika, then tried deep right on second-and-seven at 1:55. Blathers intercepted it and returned thirty-nine yards, leaving Lavender six yards from another touchdown. The Wails asked Hobbes for two runs: one yard left, then five up the middle for the score at 1:43. Another extra point made it 32–21.

Hobbes finished with 122 yards on twenty carries and two touchdowns. His longest run was twelve yards, an unusually clear illustration of how his total accumulated: repeated useful gains rather than one exceptional sprint. “Twelve was apparently the ceiling,” he said. “I kept checking.” Lavender could afford that kind of small joke after a fourth quarter in which his steady rushing had supported two long drives and completed the short one.

The Tide’s final possession ended on downs after two unsuccessful throws toward Quilava. Frosmoth took the last two kneel-downs. Cerulean finished ahead in total yards, 378–339, but Lavender converted six of eleven third downs against four of ten for the Tide and threw one interception against two. The Wails also gained 138 rushing yards as a team and scored three rushing touchdowns. Those differences explain the result more precisely than a broad claim that one team simply wanted the game more.

Lavender is 10–5 and has won three straight. It visits Violet next with People Eater still carrying a one-week injury report and Mr. Clanky seven. The available offense has now produced a road comeback through several contributors, though the scoreless third quarter remains part of the same evidence. Cerulean falls to 7–8 before hosting Saffron, a particularly difficult opponent after the Psi Corps’ seventy-point win over Blackthorn. Farigiraf’s explosive connections give the Tide something to build on; the two interceptions and fourth-quarter stops are immediate work for the next preparation.

art.alt: Arcanine #58, Frosmoth #15. Hobbes and Frosmoth helped Lavender leave Cerulean with its tenth victory.

articles.title: Rustboro keeps the ball, finishes late and closes on Petalburg
articles.dek: Philly Gabite scores twice, Shawn Watzon spreads 263 passing yards among nine receivers, and the Stone answer a 98-yard return in a 32–14 win over Canalave.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Rustboro spent much of the first half keeping the ball and very little of it adding to the score. The Stone ran an eighty-seven-yard touchdown drive, then a seventy-seven-yard possession that ended on downs. They led Canalave 7–0 at the break. By the finish, their patience had produced five touchdowns, a 32–14 victory and a much more useful place in the division race: one game behind Petalburg, with the Pride coming to Rustboro next.

Philly Gabite carried seventeen times for eighty-four yards and two touchdowns. Shawn Watzon completed twenty-four of thirty-one passes for 263 yards, two scores and no interceptions. The Stone gained 412 yards against Canalave’s 129, earned twenty-two first downs to six and never punted. Those advantages required repeated decisions to continue on fourth down, followed by enough execution to make the decisions worthwhile.

Tyler Scarboro was asked afterward about keeping his offense on the field. “People talk about possession like owning a chair,” the Rustboro coach said. “You can sit in it all afternoon and accomplish nothing. We had that nineteen-play drive and got no points. Nice chair. The other drives, we finished. That is the part I liked.” Rustboro had moved the ball on both first-half possessions but finished only one with points.

Rustboro improved to 9–6 after the previous week’s 41–7 loss at Sunyshore. Canalave fell to 7–8, two games behind Eterna in Sinnoh West. Neither team had secured a playoff berth when the afternoon ended. The Stone can qualify with a win or tie against Petalburg. The Bulwark host Snowpoint next and need to improve their position before a final trip to Oreburgh.
The long possessions that built a narrow lead

Canalave’s opening series reached third-and-one before Slowking was stopped for no gain by Smoke Break, Rustboro’s Gigalith. Vikavolt punted, Joe returned it six yards, and the Stone began an eighty-seven-yard march. Watzon converted third-and-four with five yards to Sudowoodo and another third-and-four with nine to SEARED BITE. The drive became more demanding when a six-yard pass to Nidorina left fourth-and-four.

Watzon answered with a nine-yard completion short left to Nuzleaf, then went deep right to the same receiver for twenty-two. A ten-yard throw to Diggersby preceded Philly Gabite’s two-yard touchdown run to the right with forty-six seconds left in the quarter. Fifteen plays had produced seven points. The Stone had used short completions to remain on the field and a deeper throw to accelerate the final portion of the possession.

“They put the ball there, I finished it,” Gabite said. “People can discuss how many yards looked impressive. Two was the correct number.” His longest run on the day was eleven yards. The value came from repeated useful carries and two finishes near the goal line, rather than one long run that could disguise an otherwise unproductive afternoon.

Rustboro’s next possession lasted nineteen plays and covered seventy-seven yards, yet ended with Watchog losing a yard on fourth-and-one. Medicham made the stop with forty seconds left in the half. Earlier in the drive Watzon had converted fourth-and-one with a three-yard run, and Watchog had gained seven on fourth-and-two. Canalave finally made the fourth-down resistance decisive. The result kept a game of uneven possession within one touchdown.

That sequence gives the halftime score its proper context. Canalave had twice punted, while Rustboro’s only two first-half possessions had consumed substantial ground and time. The Bulwark defense was spending long stretches on the field and still protecting a manageable deficit. Froslass broke up two consecutive throws late in the second drive, and Medicham supplied its ending. Rustboro’s ability to continue drives had been established; its ability to finish every one of them had not.
Manectric answers in one return

The Stone opened the second half with another seventy-five-yard touchdown drive. Passimian sacked Watzon for eight yards, but the quarterback recovered the possession through Gengar: five yards short right, then twenty-eight deep through the middle on third-and-thirteen. The drive finished with a one-yard pass short right to Nidorina on third-and-one. Gorebyss’s kick put Rustboro ahead 14–0.

Manectric returned the ensuing kickoff ninety-eight yards for a touchdown. The game log places the kickoff at 2:22 in the third quarter; Vikavolt’s extra point made it 14–7. Rustboro had required twelve plays to create its touchdown. Canalave’s return unit answered without involving the offense at all. Manectric finished with 180 yards and a touchdown on four returns, the largest individual source of field position and scoring opportunity the Bulwark had.

body.alt: Manectric #14. Manectric returned a third-quarter kickoff ninety-eight yards for Canalave’s first touchdown.
body.caption: Manectric returned a third-quarter kickoff ninety-eight yards for Canalave’s first touchdown.

body.text: “The people in front of me did their work,” Manectric said. “I got the part everybody remembers. I would rather we had given them a win to remember with it.” The return mattered immediately because it prevented Rustboro’s long drives from creating a comfortable advantage. It also left Canalave dependent on finding another kind of scoring possession before the Stone finished again.

Rustboro’s answer began with Gabite running eleven yards right and Watzon finding SEARED BITE for sixteen on a deep throw to that side. Delcatty then sacked Watzon for four yards, helping force another fourth down. Gabite converted fourth-and-two with five yards left. The Stone kept going into the final quarter and faced fourth-and-one again, this time with a considerably larger gain available.

Watzon threw deep left to Gibby Timmy for twenty-three yards. On the next play Gabite scored from two yards out, this time through the middle, with 5:02 remaining. Cetitan blocked the extra point, leaving Rustboro ahead 20–7. The Stone had answered the return with another seventy-five-yard touchdown possession and two more fourth-down conversions. Their approach demanded execution; that drive supplied it in two different forms.
The six-point game that lasted one possession

Canalave finally produced its own sustained scoring response. Slowking found Grafaiai deep right for thirty-one yards, then completed throws to Manectric for ten, Seviper for twelve and Torterra for sixteen. Delcatty scored on a one-yard run through the middle at 3:59. Vikavolt converted, and the Bulwark were within 20–14 despite the large differences in total yards and first downs.

Four of Slowking’s five completions came on that drive. He finished five-for-thirteen for ninety-four yards, with neither a touchdown pass nor an interception. The six-play scoring possession showed what Canalave could do when it completed throws beyond the initial line of defense. The rest of the afternoon gave the Bulwark too few such sequences: they converted one of five third downs and rushed for thirty-five yards on twelve attempts.

Gengar returned the next squib kick thirty yards, and Watzon immediately found Gibby Timmy deep right for forty-one. Gabite followed with runs of seven and six. After Watzon lost two yards, Watchog scored through the middle from nine yards out at the two-minute mark. The two-point attempt failed when Kecleon broke up the pass to SEARED BITE. Rustboro led 26–14, having answered Canalave’s only offensive touchdown with another of its own.

body.alt: Archeops #99, Porygon-Z #37. Gibby Timmy’s forty-one-yard reception helped Rustboro extend its fourth-quarter lead.
body.caption: Gibby Timmy’s forty-one-yard reception helped Rustboro extend its fourth-quarter lead.

body.text: “I just tried to get through what was there,” Watchog said. “The line and the passes had done so much before that. I did not want to waste it.” He finished with forty-seven yards and the touchdown on twelve carries. Together with Gabite, he supplied 131 yards on twenty-nine carries. Rustboro finished with thirty-five team rushing attempts and 149 yards, enough production to support its short passing game.

The Bulwark’s next four passes fell incomplete. Joe and Frosmoth each broke one up, and Rustboro took over on downs. Gabite supplied three carries before Watzon found Sudowoodo short right for a ten-yard touchdown on third-and-four with 1:30 left. Gorebyss missed the extra point wide left. Three fourth-quarter touchdowns had supplied eighteen points, taking the game from 14–7 at the quarter break to its final 32–14 score.
A useful win before two division opponents

Watzon spread his twenty-four completions among nine receivers. Gibby Timmy led with sixty-four yards on two catches; SEARED BITE caught five for fifty-three, Gengar four for fifty and Nuzleaf three for forty-one. The late explosive throws mattered, but the distribution explains how Rustboro kept finding another answer when an earlier attempt failed. “Stay with the next play,” Watzon said. “There was usually something there.”

The Stone also received substantial recorded work up front: Aggron had nine pancakes and Crustle seven, each with a ninety-seven percent block-win figure. Canalave registered two sacks and broke up passes, but could not consistently finish possessions with the ball changing hands. Rustboro converted eight of thirteen third downs and repeatedly survived the fourth downs that followed the others.

Milotic’s new six-week injury designation complicates the next assignment for the Stone; the record does not identify an exact injury time. Petalburg arrives with a chance to clinch Hoenn West by winning, while Rustboro can secure a berth by avoiding defeat and keep a stronger division challenge alive by winning. Dewford follows in Week 18. Rustboro has two home games left, both against teams directly involved in deciding its postseason position.

articles.title: Cinnabar’s five touchdown drives overwhelm Mt. Silver
articles.dek: Gholdengo completed thirty-three passes as the Blaze won 38–24. Arcanine scored twice before a three-week injury report complicated the next assignment.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Cinnabar scored touchdowns on its first five full offensive possessions against Mt. Silver. The Blaze went seventy-three yards, eighty-one, seventy-eight, seventy-two and eighty, with a halftime kneel separating the third march from the fourth. Gholdengo kept completing passes, the backs kept finishing, and an opponent that arrived 13–1 eventually ran out of immediate answers. Cinnabar won 38–24 and reached ten wins with a second consecutive victory over a division leader.

I have spent enough time asking Blaine’s team to begin its good work before the score becomes desperate. This afternoon supplies the requested correction. Cinnabar led 21–14 at halftime, scored fourteen unanswered points in the third quarter and made the Reds chase a twenty-one-point deficit. The Blaze beat Blackthorn 31–19 a week ago. Their current argument includes two substantial opponents and sixty-nine points scored against them.

Gholdengo completed thirty-three of forty-one passes for 357 yards and two touchdowns without an interception. Arcanine ran for fifty yards and two scores, adding fifty receiving yards. Buizel scored on the ground and through the air. The offense gained 424 yards, converted five of eight third downs and punted once. Those are the measures of how often Cinnabar made the next possession useful.

“We expected to move the ball,” Gholdengo said. “When they answered, we went back to work. I wanted the next throw.” The quarterback’s confidence had plenty of support. Nine different teammates caught a pass, and the offense recovered from the few situations in which the Reds seemed close to ending a drive.
Cinnabar answered two Lynch touchdowns

The Blaze’s first possession began with two short-left completions to Thievul and included nineteen yards through the air to Arcanine. Exploud’s fifteen-yard catch brought the offense close enough for Buizel to finish. He ran right for seven yards with 3:20 left in the first quarter, and Charjabug’s extra point supplied a 7–0 lead.

Garshawn Lynch answered emphatically. His thirty-yard run began the next Mt. Silver drive, and his twelve-yard touchdown up the middle finished it. The Reds had moved sixty-six yards to tie the game. Lynch would finish with 113 rushing yards on eight carries, a striking amount of production from a limited number of attempts. He gave Connor McLarren a way to match Cinnabar early even as the passing game struggled to find regular completions.

The next Blaze possession immediately encountered trouble. Blayz Matthews sacked Gholdengo for six yards, and Mach Singltery broke up the following pass. On third-and-sixteen, Gholdengo found Archaludon deep right for twenty-five. Cinnabar later converted third-and-four with a twenty-four-yard completion to Exploud. Two chances to end the drive became large gains instead.

Thievul caught the one-yard touchdown with 4:37 left in the second quarter, completing an eighty-one-yard march. Lynch answered again, this time breaking a forty-five-yard touchdown run through the middle. Mt. Silver had tied it at fourteen. The Reds were still keeping pace, but Cinnabar had already demonstrated that forcing a long third down would not automatically send its offense away.

body.alt: Garchomp #22. Garshawn Lynch’s forty-five-yard touchdown run brought Mt. Silver level at 14–14 after the extra point.
body.caption: Garshawn Lynch’s forty-five-yard touchdown run brought Mt. Silver level at 14–14 after the extra point.

body.text: Buizel finished the difficult possession

Gholdengo opened the ensuing drive with two incompletions intended for Arcanine. He returned to the same receiver on third-and-ten and gained twenty-three yards. That decision kept a seventy-eight-yard touchdown possession alive and began another sequence in which the Blaze distributed the work. Thievul, Wigglytuff and Skiploom supplied catches; Gholdengo himself converted a third-and-one with a two-yard run.

Near the end of the half, Cinnabar faced third-and-eleven. A pass to Buizel had been broken up, and a short throw to Arcanine lost a yard. Gholdengo then found Buizel deep left for a fourteen-yard touchdown with forty-five seconds remaining. The Blaze had moved ahead 21–14 by recovering from two distinct long-yardage situations on the same drive.

“I wanted the next chance as soon as the first one was gone,” Buizel said. “There was another play to run.” His eagerness was rewarded. He had finished the opening drive on the ground and now finished the last meaningful Cinnabar drive of the half through the air. Two different assignments had produced touchdowns from the same back.

body.alt: Buizel #16. Buizel caught a fourteen-yard touchdown pass late in the first half.
body.caption: Buizel caught a fourteen-yard touchdown pass late in the first half.

body.text: Mt. Silver gained nine yards on its next first down, then encountered number 48 Thievul twice. He broke up consecutive throws to Gregar Jenings on second-and-one and third-and-one. The Reds punted, and Cinnabar knelt to end the half. The receiver wearing 45 had scored earlier; the defender wearing 48 had helped protect the lead. Keeping the two Thievul contributions separate improves the account considerably.
Arcanine turned seven points into twenty-one

Cinnabar opened the third quarter with three consecutive completions: eleven yards to Exploud, twenty-seven to number 45 Thievul and seventeen to Beautifly. Arcanine then ran three times, finishing the drive with a five-yard touchdown to the right. The offense had gone seventy-two yards without facing a third down and moved ahead 28–14.

The Reds found a first down on their answer but stalled when Mawile sacked Jacoby Brizzet on third-and-two. After the punt, Cinnabar drove eighty yards in six plays. Thievul caught fourteen and nineteen yards around Archaludon’s twenty-seven-yard reception. Arcanine finished with a seventeen-yard run to the left, and Charjabug made it 35–14 with 1:04 remaining in the quarter.

Arcanine’s current injury report lists three weeks, a substantial cost attached to a productive afternoon. The recorded game does not timestamp the injury. His fifty rushing yards, fifty receiving yards and two touchdowns describe what Cinnabar received here; they also explain why Blaine’s preparation for Celadon now includes replacing more than a single kind of offensive work.

“The other guys did a lot to get us there,” Arcanine said. “I’m happy the runs helped.” The reserved answer leaves room to recognize those contributors. Thievul caught ten of eleven targets for ninety-six yards and a touchdown. Archaludon caught all three of his targets for fifty-nine. Gholdengo repeatedly found useful gains before asking the backfield to finish.
Mt. Silver recovered ten points, then ran out of time

The strangest turnover sequence arrived late in the third quarter. Number 48 Thievul intercepted a deep-right pass, then fumbled, and Gregar Jenings recovered for Mt. Silver. The Reds retained an opportunity, but Primeape sacked Brizzet for seven yards on the next snap. Crem Ftzpatrik completed a four-yard pass and then threw incomplete. Mt. Silver punted again.

Brizzet returned to the passing record in the fourth quarter and led a seventy-five-yard touchdown drive. A thirty-one-yard completion to Ariados converted third-and-ten, and a four-yard pass to Lynch finished the march. Lynch had supplied both early rushing touchdowns and now the receiving score. The extra point reduced the margin to 35–21.

Cinnabar then supplied an avoidable opening. Arcanine fumbled the ensuing kickoff return, and Weepinbell recovered for Mt. Silver. The Reds moved the ball far enough for his twenty-three-yard field goal, cutting the deficit to eleven. Glalie recovered the subsequent onside kick for Cinnabar, and the Blaze used their next possession to reach a forty-three-yard Charjabug field goal with 1:59 left. The margin was fourteen again.

“They were considerate enough to let us back near it,” McLarren said. “Unfortunately, they had already spent three quarters completing passes. We should try being less hospitable when somebody needs sixteen yards.” His defense allowed twenty first downs. Brizzet finished sixteen of thirty-five for 172 yards, one touchdown and one interception; the Reds’ passing game could not sustain the pace their early rushing explosions had established.

Mt. Silver also received a twelve-week injury report for Ariados after his five catches for fifty-six yards. Tic Thorpe and Josh Alakazam remain unavailable with five and six reported weeks respectively. The Reds travel to Azalea at 13–2 with both offensive availability and defensive third-down execution demanding attention. Cinnabar visits Celadon at 10–5, carrying two consecutive wins and a newly difficult backfield adjustment. Blaine has strong evidence to build on: five sustained touchdown drives against a thirteen-win opponent, with thirty-three completed passes doing much of the work.

articles.title: Mauville has earned a harder test
articles.dek: Three consecutive wins have carried the Dynamos to 8–7. Dewford will test whether the passing game and pressure can travel together.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Mauville has won three consecutive games by three different kinds of margin: one point at Lavaridge, six in overtime at Veilstone, and thirty-seven against Snowpoint. I want Wattson to preserve the progression without treating the final score as proof that every problem has disappeared. The Dynamos have reached 8–7. They now visit a Dewford team with nine wins and a fresh 24–10 victory. The quality of the next offensive possession matters more than how often someone repeats the word momentum.

There is enough good football in the Snowpoint result to make a specific case. Togekiss completed eighteen of twenty-seven for 198 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. Volbeat recorded four sacks. Bibarel supplied sixty-three yards on fourteen carries. Those contributions gave Mauville productive passing, a meaningful rushing supplement and pressure capable of disrupting the opponent. I want those functions together again at Dewford.
Three receivers finished different jobs

Mothim caught six passes for fifty-four yards and a touchdown. Tangrowth caught four for sixty and a touchdown. Luvdisc’s one reception gained nine yards and scored. The three touchdown passes went to three players, with substantially different workloads. A staff preparing for Mauville has to consider more than the largest receiving-yardage entry.

That distribution is useful because it gives Togekiss more than one reasonable place to complete a possession. Mothim contributed repeated catches, Tangrowth gained fifteen yards per reception, and Luvdisc finished his single recorded opportunity. Those are descriptions of production, not a claim about routes the totals cannot reveal. The next preparation should ask how to make each job available against Dewford’s actual coverage.

Togekiss also kept the interception column empty. That deserves emphasis for a club that won its previous game in overtime and the one before that by a point. Mauville has already spent enough afternoons needing the final result to remain available. An offense that retains possession gives its defense a better chance to decide the game through ordinary stops instead of constant rescue work.
Volbeat supplied four sacks

Four sacks from one defender are difficult to overlook, even if a reader begins with the thirty-seven points on the scoreboard. Drednaw added another. Snowpoint’s Drampa threw for 115 yards and an interception, while Dragapult recorded the interception for Mauville. Pressure and coverage both appear in the outcome. Volbeat’s second sack came on third-and-two in the first quarter; his fourth came on fourth-and-eight with fifty-three seconds left. The pressure ended useful chances as well as reducing the yardage total.

Dragapult made the third quarter decisive in two different roles. He returned an interception seventy yards for a touchdown at 4:02, then returned the ensuing Snowpoint punt eighty-three yards for another score at 3:02. Those fourteen points took Mauville from 17–0 to 31–0 without an offensive touchdown between them. The offense’s three touchdown passes deserve credit, and the return work deserves its own account.

I like that Wattson can now show his players a win in which the defense did not need the offense to match every score. Snowpoint scored none. The preceding overtime win at Veilstone required twenty-nine Mauville points to beat twenty-three. The Dynamos have won with different requirements, and the latest defensive response gives them something better to practice toward than merely surviving another close finish.

“Four is good,” Volbeat said. “The next quarterback still gets a fresh game. I want to get moving again.” That impatience suits his afternoon. The coaching task is to direct it: reproduce the useful pressure without assuming that the next opponent will present the same chances.
Dewford can ask a different question

The Breakers’ Frosmoth threw for 193 yards and two touchdowns without an interception against Oreburgh. Swellow caught ninety-two yards and a touchdown. Dewford arrives with a completed offensive performance of its own, and its nine wins give the matchup a direct consequence for the teams currently occupying the conference’s lower playoff places. Mauville cannot plan as if another 115-yard passing opponent is guaranteed.

The Dynamos’ season totals make the defensive challenge especially clear. Mauville has allowed 1,366 rushing yards across fifteen games, a little over ninety-one per game. Its own rushing attack has supplied 822, just under fifty-five per game. Those totals do not predict the next score, but they identify a persistent difference in how much ground production each side of a Mauville game has received.

Bibarel’s sixty-three yards against Snowpoint are therefore worth preserving. They exceed the club’s season per-game rushing average before even adding the other carriers. The offense does not need to turn into a completely different system to give Togekiss useful help. It needs enough reliable rushing work that the passer can reach the next down with options.

Mauville has scored 228 points and allowed 228. That even season total includes a three-game stretch in which it outscored opponents 77–33, so the earlier weeks still exert a substantial influence on the overall record. I would credit the improvement and keep asking whether it holds against a stronger immediate challenge. Beat Dewford through clean possessions and repeatable defensive work, and Wattson will have a better argument than a single impressive shutout.

articles.title: Violet has made the next Sunday consequential
articles.dek: The Falcons have climbed to 8–7 with consecutive wins. Lavender arrives while Falkner adjusts to Maractus’s two-week absence.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Violet lost three straight games from Week 12 through Week 14. The scores were 16–3 at Olivine, 30–17 against Blackthorn and 13–10 against Cianwood. The Falcons had opportunities to make that stretch less damaging, particularly in the last of those games, and finished it with another defeat. Two weeks later, they have won twice and reached 8–7. Lavender is coming to town. Their next home game now carries a much more hopeful set of conversations.

I prefer to begin with what changed in the results. Violet held Viridian to three points in Week 15, then scored twenty to beat Fuchsia by three. The Falcons found a comfortable defensive win and followed it with a close road win. Neither result can repair the losses already on the schedule. Both have given the players another reason to prepare as if the remaining games can reward them.

The current conference table still places Violet outside the seven playoff positions. Olivine and Vermilion also stand at 8–7 and occupy the sixth and seventh seeds. A winning record has improved the Falcons’ position without settling their place. That is an awkward combination for anyone trying to celebrate responsibly, but it is a considerable improvement on another week spent explaining why a manageable game got away.
Samurott made the catches count

At Fuchsia, Samurott caught seven passes for ninety-six yards and a touchdown. Iron Jugulis completed sixteen passes overall for 176 yards, so the receiver accounted for nearly half the completions and more than half the passing yardage. The quarterback finished with one touchdown pass and no interceptions. Their twelve-yard touchdown connection, short right with 4:57 left, supplied Violet’s final lead after Fuchsia had moved ahead 17–13. There is a clear partnership to retain from this game.

“He gave me chances I could finish,” Samurott said. “The other catches kept us moving too. I wanted mine to help.” The gentle answer fits a performance that can be appreciated without turning it into a demand that one receiver supply the entire offense next week. Zangoose added two catches for nineteen yards alongside sixty-nine rushing yards. Furret caught thirty-one yards. Useful contributions came from several places.

Falkner can ask that distribution to remain available against Lavender. Samurott’s ninety-six yards are an important piece of the preparation, but a defense that studies the same numbers will have its own response. Keeping Zangoose involved on the ground and preserving the secondary completions gives Iron Jugulis more than a single solution when the first attractive throw is covered.
Maractus leaves a specific role to fill

Maractus contributed thirty-one yards on three carries and a rushing touchdown, plus a three-yard reception. His fifteen-yard touchdown up the middle with thirty-two seconds left in the first half helped Violet reach halftime tied 10–10. The new injury report lists a two-week absence; the record does not timestamp the injury. Violet loses a player who contributed to both the rushing and receiving record in the win, with a particularly valuable finishing play on the ground.

That absence should be discussed in terms of work. Someone must take the available offensive opportunities, and the staff must decide whether the same player can handle all of them. Zangoose’s eleven carries and two receptions show what he actually supplied against Fuchsia. They do not establish that he will automatically absorb every missing Maractus assignment. Falkner has a decision to make before anyone can describe the replacement as confirmed.

“We have to prepare the players who can go,” Falkner said. “Maractus helped us win. The next group needs to understand what we are asking.” It is a measured response to a familiar late-season problem. The victory has given Violet something to protect, and the injury has immediately added another task to protecting it.
Lavender brings evidence of its own

Lavender has won three in a row, beating Azalea 13–3, Celadon 20–17 and Cerulean 32–21. The Wails have done it while their passing arrangements changed, and Mr. Clanky remains out seven reported weeks. Frosmoth threw for 201 yards at Cerulean; Hobbes rushed for 122. Travis Scarboro’s team has demonstrated useful answers rather than simply asking everyone to be patient about an absence.

The Falcons should take the rushing contribution seriously. Hobbes’s 122 yards would be significant in any matchup, and Violet has allowed 1,247 rushing yards in fifteen games. Keeping Lavender from repeatedly reaching comfortable follow-up downs would help the home defense ask more of its replacement passer. That is a football assignment a player can prepare for, regardless of how the rest of the conference’s games turn out.

Violet has scored 228 points and allowed 236 this season. Consecutive victories have brought the team close to even in that measure and above even in the record. I am reluctant to announce a transformation on the strength of beating Viridian and Fuchsia. I am equally reluctant to dismiss two wins that gave these players a meaningful game against a ten-win division rival. They have earned that opportunity. Falkner’s next week will be spent deciding how to use it with one fewer recent touchdown scorer available.

articles.title: Flannery, keep giving Fearow useful chances
articles.dek: Lavaridge has scored 58 points in two victories. Its passing attack finally gave a five-interception defense enough help to win comfortably.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Flannery watched Lavaridge score ten points in consecutive losses. Sootopolis beat the Inferno 14–10; Mauville beat them 11–10. Those were games in which one more productive offensive possession could have made a substantial difference. Now Lavaridge has won 20–13 at Eterna and beaten Pastoria 38–10. I would like the staff to retain the part where its offense makes the defense’s work rewarding.

Fearow caught six passes for 144 yards and three touchdowns against the Waves. Delphox threw four touchdown passes without an interception. Venusaur intercepted three passes, while Malamar and Musharna intercepted one each. The result involved an offense capable of scoring repeatedly and a defense that supplied five interceptions. Thirty-eight points becomes considerably easier to understand when the two departments cooperate like that.

The Inferno are still 6–9. Their season has included enough difficult afternoons to keep a flattering two-week summary from passing for a complete account. They have scored 232 points and allowed 325. I am asking Flannery to make this improvement useful, starting with Fortree’s visit. Another afternoon of ten points would be an especially irritating response to discovering that the team can produce substantially more.
Fearow supplied more than half the passing yards

The arithmetic is quite friendly to the receiver. Delphox threw for 263 yards; Aromatisse added eight on one completion. Fearow accounted for 144 of those 271 passing yards, more than half of the total, with twenty-four yards per catch. Three of his six receptions scored. Lavaridge found a way to turn a small number of completed opportunities into an enormous share of its scoring work.

That does not establish that every future pass to Fearow should travel twenty-four yards or finish in the end zone. It establishes that a receiver produced a remarkable afternoon when given opportunities to finish. I want the offense to investigate which parts it can reproduce against Fortree while accepting that the next defense gets to participate in the investigation.

“I was just trying to be ready when the ball came,” Fearow said. “Three touchdowns is more attention than I expected.” His bashful answer is charming. His production warrants the attention anyway. Receivers are permitted to dislike the interview and still catch the ball when the game asks for it.

Delphox completed eighteen of twenty-eight. Mothim caught six for sixty-five yards. Arbok caught four for thirty and a touchdown. Stantler added three catches for thirty-two alongside forty rushing yards. Fearow was the largest contribution, and the other completions helped make the offense more than one spectacular line in the box score.
Five interceptions deserve their own credit

Venusaur recorded three of the five interceptions against Farigiraf. His first interception set up Fearow’s twenty-one-yard touchdown on the next offensive snap, and his third became a seventy-one-yard touchdown return in the third quarter. The defense supplied both opportunities and points directly. Fearow later added a fifty-two-yard touchdown catch, his third score, with 4:14 left. Lavaridge had reached 38–0 before Pastoria scored.

The danger in reviewing this game is to assume five interceptions are now a normal weekly allowance. Flannery should praise every one of them and prepare for Fortree as if the defense will need ordinary stops too. Lavaridge has allowed more than twenty-one points per game over the season. The ten conceded to Pastoria are an improvement worth studying, not a reason to erase the previous games.

Mantine’s new one-week absence adds another defensive adjustment. The injury report provides a duration, not a promise about exactly how the remaining assignments will be redistributed. A staff that just received a major defensive performance still needs to prepare the available players. Success does not grant an exemption from having the right people ready for the next snap.
Fortree supplies an immediate test of discipline

The Skyhawks have allowed 389 points and just lost 27–7 to Hearthome. That makes the matchup attractive for a Lavaridge offense that has scored fifty-eight across its last two wins. It also makes it easy to mistake preparation for an exercise in deciding how many points to expect. Fortree remains a team capable of making Lavaridge waste a possession if the Inferno oblige.

I want Delphox to preserve the clean interception line and the distribution that supported Fearow’s day. I want Stantler’s rushing work to keep the passing game from carrying every ordinary down. I want the defense to pursue takeaways while also being able to end a drive that does not include one. Those are demands supported by what Lavaridge just did well and by what its full season says it still needs.

Flannery has won at Eterna, a division leader, and then beaten Pastoria comfortably. That is enough progress to deserve a more ambitious request than merely keeping the next score close. Build another complete offensive afternoon against Fortree. The players have just shown that they can give their defense something better than ten points to defend.

articles.title: The Rook Board: choose the backfield job before the back
articles.dek: Stakataka leads the fullback evaluations, Miltank leads the halfbacks, and several close comparisons deserve identical workouts.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: Zapapico’s Stakataka and Blackthorn’s Miltank lead two different evaluations. Stakataka is a listed fullback with an 87–99 disclosed range, twenty-seven bench repetitions and a 5.23 forty. Miltank is a halfback with a 65–93 range, twenty-two bench repetitions and a 4.72 forty. Putting them on the same backfield board is useful only if we retain the jobs those numbers are helping us investigate.

I rank Stakataka first because the strength of his disclosed fullback profile deserves the earliest detailed examination. Miltank is my first halfback, with Zangoose the close comparison. A team needing a runner should compare those two directly rather than assuming that the first name in a combined ranking solves its vacancy. A team needing a blocker should compare Stakataka, Druddigon and Parasect on the assignments it actually intends to call.

The current league supplied a helpful range of backfield work this week. Mossdeep received 121 rushing yards from Poury Holt; Lavender received 122 from Hobbes. Violet received rushing and receiving work from Zangoose, then lost Maractus to a reported two-week absence after he contributed a rushing touchdown. Those examples explain why staffs should evaluate carrying, catching, blocking and reserve readiness separately. They do not establish that any rookie below can immediately reproduce the production.

My twelve-player order uses disclosed ranges and combine results. The ranges describe uncertainty in the current evaluation; they are not promises of growth or eventual performance. I would give the close pairs the same drills, the same protection questions and the same chances to catch the ball before asking the board to become more precise.

prospects.name: Stakataka
prospects.analysis: Zapapico’s Stakataka begins with an 87–99 disclosed band and twenty-seven bench repetitions. At 5.23 in the forty, he demands a precise job: evaluate the blocking and short-area contribution before imagining a space runner.
prospects.concern: A high listed fullback range does not answer every blocking assignment or establish a different position.
prospects.projection: First fullback evaluation for a club with a meaningful blocking role.

prospects.name: Miltank
prospects.analysis: Blackthorn’s Miltank leads my halfbacks: 65–93, a 4.72 forty, twenty-two bench repetitions and a 6.58 cone. The combination gives me several useful questions for a complete backfield workout.
prospects.concern: The workout does not establish ball security, receiving reliability or protection recognition.
prospects.projection: Leading halfback comparison for a club evaluating a larger offensive workload.

prospects.name: Druddigon
prospects.analysis: Po State’s Druddigon offers a 74–99 fullback band, twenty-three bench repetitions and a 7.01 cone. I want him and Stakataka taking identical lead-block and protection assignments.
prospects.concern: The bands overlap substantially, and bench strength alone cannot settle blocking technique.
prospects.projection: High-priority fullback competitor whose role should be established before draft day.

prospects.name: Zangoose
prospects.analysis: Opelucid’s Zangoose has a 63–91 band, 4.75 forty and 6.60 cone. Those results sit close enough to Miltank’s to justify a direct comparison rather than a confident claim of separation.
prospects.concern: Small testing differences cannot establish a durable advantage in live rushing decisions.
prospects.projection: Main halfback alternative to Miltank, with receiving and protection work still to examine.

prospects.name: Parasect
prospects.analysis: Cyllage’s Parasect brings a 64–92 fullback band and twenty bench repetitions. His 5.05 forty gives a different movement question from the slower top fullbacks.
prospects.concern: Timed movement is not evidence that he will identify and complete a moving block.
prospects.projection: A fullback comparison for clubs that ask the position to reach targets beyond the initial collision.

prospects.name: Ariados
prospects.analysis: Seafolk State’s Ariados pairs a 61–89 band with seventeen bench repetitions and a 5.06 forty. The numbers merit a close look at the actual work between runner and blocker.
prospects.concern: The forty is very close to Parasect’s; the overlap prevents a simple workout-based verdict.
prospects.projection: A second cluster of fullback candidates after the leading evaluations.

prospects.name: Kecleon
prospects.analysis: Pyrite School of Mines’ Kecleon has a 60–88 band and a 6.96 cone. I would compare him with the other Kecleon prospects on the same assignment sheet, keeping their identities separate.
prospects.concern: A quicker cone does not by itself prove better recognition or contact work.
prospects.projection: A movement-oriented fullback evaluation within a tightly grouped set.

prospects.name: Kecleon
prospects.analysis: Twinleaf’s Kecleon is twenty-one, with a 59–87 band, 5.09 forty and fourteen bench repetitions. His range overlaps Pyrite’s almost completely.
prospects.concern: The younger age does not guarantee a faster development rate or better eventual player.
prospects.projection: A close alternative requiring a football-workout comparison rather than a school preference.

prospects.name: Nidorino
prospects.analysis: Cherrygrove’s Nidorino offers a 52–80 halfback band, 4.90 forty and 6.67 cone. I would test whether his useful work comes from ordinary rushing decisions or a narrower complementary assignment.
prospects.concern: The reported range remains broad; testing does not establish readiness for heavy usage.
prospects.projection: Halfback competition below the leading Miltank and Zangoose evaluations.

prospects.name: Deerling
prospects.analysis: Mid-Galar State’s Deerling has a 49–77 band and 6.53 cone, the quickest cone among these selected halfbacks. The 4.89 forty gives another useful movement comparison.
prospects.concern: A strong cone cannot promise receiving skill, durability or success through contact.
prospects.projection: A complementary-back evaluation with open questions about the broader role.

prospects.name: Kecleon
prospects.analysis: Lilycove’s Kecleon brings a 53–81 band, 5.01 forty and seventeen bench repetitions. That is the quickest forty of the three Kecleon prospects here, though his disclosed band is lower.
prospects.concern: A few hundredths in a workout cannot resolve the larger uncertainty in actual contribution.
prospects.projection: A third Kecleon comparison for teams seeking a particular fullback assignment.

prospects.name: Numel
prospects.analysis: Hearthome’s Numel is twenty-one, with a 46–74 band, 5.01 forty and thirteen bench repetitions. I want a clear developmental job before I become enthusiastic about the favorable end of the range.
prospects.concern: The upper boundary is an uncertainty limit, not a promised future rating.
prospects.projection: A later fullback evaluation after the immediate role and roster competition are defined.

articles.title: Injury Report: Milotic and Seviper miss the division showdown
articles.dek: New losses affect Rustboro, Petalburg, Cinnabar and Mt. Silver; the full league comparison separates injuries, recovery countdowns and cleared reports.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Rustboro and Petalburg lose contributors before their meeting

Rustboro cornerback Milotic has a new six-week injury report, and Petalburg tight end Seviper has a new one-week report. They are consequential absences before the division rivals meet. Seviper caught five passes for forty-three yards against Eterna and has forty-nine catches for 494 yards this season. Farigiraf and Vikavolt are established receiving alternatives, but an expanded role is analysis rather than a confirmed new assignment. Rustboro’s coverage group must adjust while Iron Valiant looks for those remaining options.

The Stone continue without My Way, Son, whose reported absence has fallen from three weeks to two. Philly Gabite and Watchog combined for 131 rushing yards and three touchdowns against Canalave. That recorded production gives Rustboro a demonstrated available backfield before Petalburg; Milotic’s replacement work remains to be established.
Cinnabar and Mt. Silver absorb new offensive losses

Cinnabar’s Arcanine is newly out three reported weeks after contributing fifty rushing yards, fifty receiving yards and two rushing touchdowns against Mt. Silver. Seismitoad remains out one week. Buizel scored both a rushing and a receiving touchdown in the same win, providing one observed contributor as the Blaze prepare for Celadon. That does not establish an automatic promotion or promise the same workload.

Mt. Silver tight end Ariados has a new twelve-week report after five catches for fifty-six yards at Cinnabar. The Reds already have Tic Thorpe out five weeks and Josh Alakazam six. Jacoby Brizzet supplied most of the passing against the Blaze, while Garshawn Lynch produced 113 rushing yards and three total touchdowns. Before Azalea, the available rushing production offers support for a passing group that has lost another contributor. Foo Warner still has one week; cornerback Ninjask has cleared his previous positive recovery counter.
New injuries across the playoff races

Olivine receiver Magmar is newly out two weeks and tight end Bibarel one. Magmar caught two passes for eighteen yards at Pewter; Veluza led the receiving work with seven catches for seventy-two. Stantler remains out six weeks and Beedrill fourteen. Maractus and Thievul have cleared their previous positive counters, improving the available pool without confirming either player’s next assignment. Olivine hosts Cianwood, which continues to list Gardevoir at one week and Haunter at three.

Violet loses slot receiver Maractus for two weeks before Lavender. He supplied thirty-one rushing yards and a touchdown against Fuchsia. Lavender still lists People Eater at one week and Mr. Clanky at seven. Frosmoth and Hobbes produced the passing and rushing foundation at Cerulean, so the Wails enter the next game with recent evidence of how their available offense can function.

Blackthorn running back Sawsbuck has a new six-week report after the defeat at Saffron. Mahogany safety Frosmoth is newly out nine weeks before the Dragons visit. Mahogany also continues to miss Watchog for sixteen weeks, Kricketune for four and Quilladin for three. Its tight ends Golduck and Jellicent have two and one weeks respectively. Grovyle’s positive counter has cleared for Blackthorn, but that change alone does not establish game participation.

Hearthome cornerback Dodrio has a new four-week report before Veilstone, while Mr. Mime remains out eight. Veilstone running back Vigoroth is newly out three. Oreburgh has three new absences before Eterna: Dusknoir five weeks, Sharpedo three and Poliwhirl twelve. The Miners also continue without fullback Swampert for three. Those receiving and coverage losses affect both sides of a matchup with a strong defensive opponent.

Celadon defensive end Deerling is newly out four weeks before Cinnabar. Lavaridge safety Mantine has a new one-week report before Fortree. These are reported recovery durations, without a diagnosis or a guaranteed return date. The records do not establish the exact play on which any injury occurred.
Cleared counters and the full league comparison

Sunyshore’s Serp Gardener and Mossdeep’s Ninjaskamara have cleared their previous positive recovery counters. Richard Furman remains out one week for Mossdeep. Pewter’s Heatmor, Cianwood’s Doduo and Canalave’s Octillery have also cleared their previous positive counters.
